title: Second-Language Learners Need SOR+
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos argues that English Learners need the same science-of-reading foundations as every other student, plus targeted language support, which she labels SOR+. Drawing on Claude Goldenberg, a systematic review of research on multilingual learners, and her own work as a reading specialist, she says the plus is not more phonics but oracy, vocabulary, transfer and writing alongside the usual components. She walks through paired routines such as decode plus discuss, look plus label, and experiment plus explain, showing how each keeps decoding at the front while building meaning. She also defends the use of peer-assisted learning and the strategic use of home language, and rejects context-first word identification as a route for ELs. The post closes by framing teachers as superheroes and mere mortals, which supports her case that one instructional approach with added support is manageable while separate but equal instruction is not.
points: SOR+ means the same foundational skills instruction all students receive, plus attention to oracy, transfer, writing and language comprehension, rather than simply more phonics.
A systematic review of K-5 multilingual learners supports peer pairing, explicit instruction and strategic use of the first language as effective practices.
Each routine pairs a SOR component with a language-building move, for example decode plus discuss so first graders learn the meaning of words like crib and shed after they can read them.
She rejects leading with context cues for ELs because decoding is the gateway to automatic word recognition and orthographic mapping.
Same-with-support instruction is more workable for teachers than separate instruction for each subgroup, and it respects the social strengths many immigrant children bring.
quotes: Now it was up to me to seat these students at the science of reading (SOR) table and serve them the foundational skills they needed while paying close attention to the additional skill development they required as part of their English Learner status: SOR+.
Spoiler alert: it’s not more phonics. It’s the same phonics we provide during beginning reading instruction for all students plus English language development.

SOR+ does not simply mean more phonics—although it can depending on the student. Rather, it means focused foundational skills instruction with support. We simply don’t have time to teach literacy components for longer than necessary. I have written elsewhere about the importance of a streamlined SOR focus for all students. This streamlining matters because it facilitates foundational skill development while creating time for sufficient reading and writing
My job is to equip each and every student with the skills to independently attack any word at any time in any context.

My first graders can effortlessly read crib and shed but rarely know what these words mean, so I provide an explanation and point to the pictures in their decodable book to help them visualize the words.
If we are being asked to offer separate but equal instruction to our various subgroups, then that really is too much for a mere mortal to handle.

If we neglect to equip our ELs with SOR strategies that serve all learners and pretend that there are more differences than similarities in how students learn, then we are doing our ELs a grave disservice.
